title: Silver and gold I have none (Acts 3:1–10)
hookLine: but what I have, I give thee: rise and walk

lines: THREE O'CLOCK, THE HOUR OF PRAYER.
cards: Anyone who drives knows the little calculation at a red light when someone with a cardboard sign walks between the cars. Do I have cash? Is the light about to change?
Do I look, or keep my eyes on the dashboard? Usually the eyes win. Looking is the hard part.
Afternoon in Jerusalem, three o'clock, the hour of prayer. Peter and John are walking up to the temple.
At one of the gates, a man who has never walked in his life is being set down, the way he is every day, to ask for money.

teach.b: Luke says he was lame from his mother's womb, carried every day to the gate of the temple called Beautiful, to beg from people going in. He sees Peter and John and asks for alms, the way he asks everyone.
Then something unusual happens. Peter, with John, fixes his eyes on him and says, look at us. The man looks up, expecting a coin.
And Peter says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, I give thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise, and walk."
Peter takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and the man's feet and ankles grow strong. He jumps up, stands, walks, and goes into the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
Everyone recognizes him: the one from the gate. Notice the order.
First, eye contact: look at us. Before anything is given, the man is seen. Then an honest no: I don't have money.

teach.h: NO GOLD, BUT WHAT I HAVE.
teach.b: Then what Peter does have, which isn't his own: the name of Jesus. Peter's not pretending to be richer than he is, or poorer either.
There's a story people tell about Thomas Aquinas visiting the pope while gold was being counted.

teach.h: SILVER AND GOLD I HAVE NONE.
teach.b: The pope said, the Church can no longer say silver and gold I have none. And Thomas answered, no, and neither can she say, rise and walk. Nobody can confirm it happened.
But it's stuck around for centuries because it names the temptation in today's line.

how: Catholics are taught the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, giving not only money but time, care, counsel and prayer to people in need.

o: Peter's word for the healed man's new walk
the name of the pool where the sick waited
the temple gate where the lame man begged

games.q: the Beautiful gate — tap the pairs.

s: Peter gave the man a coin and then healed him
silver and gold I have none; he gave what he had.
before giving anything, Peter makes eye contact
fastening his eyes on him: look at us.
the story of Aquinas and the counted gold is historically confirmed
it's a story people tell; nobody can confirm it.

games.q: you're on your way to prayer. a man who has never walked asks you for money, and you have none. what do you do?
o: look at him, and give him what you do have.
games.why: Peter says, look at us. silver and gold I have none; but what I have, I give thee: arise, and walk.

practice: Rest your hands open on your lap and ask what you can give today, not money, necessarily: time, a skill, a car with an empty seat, a listening ear, a language you speak, a kind word, your full attention.
Name two or three things quietly, and picture one person who needs one of them. If you pray, hold Peter's words, what I have, I give thee, and offer it; if you don't, just keep your hands open.

wordCard.voice: Beautiful. The gate of the temple where a man who had never walked begged every day, until Peter said, what I have, I give thee: arise and walk. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: silver and gold (Acts 3:6); both words also mean money.

carryVoice: Your line: what I have I give. It started with a look. See you tomorrow.
